To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Acetylsalycilic acid (ASA), a nonselective NSAID, abrogated the late phase of PC in the rabbit heart, but only in high doses.
ASA blocks NF-κΒ activation and the late PC effect against myocardial infraction.
ASA in high dose blocks late PC against myocardial infraction and inhibits NF-κB dependent gene expression in the preconditioned rabbit heart.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the NF-kB pathway in late PC and the influence of ASA on this pathway.
the role of NF-κb in late preconditioning.
the effect of ASA, a nonselective cyclo-oxygenase (COX) inhibitor, on the late PC effect against myocardial infarcction and on NF-κB-activation in the preconditioned heart.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

NSAIDs may be detrimental in the setting of atherosclerosis and that their use in patients with coronary artery disease should be restricted to the lowest possible doses and to the shortest duration of time.
ASA, in doses of 130 mg/kg, completely abrogates late PC against ischemic injury in the myocardium, and this effect is related to the suppression of NF-κ-B activation.
NSAIDs, including acetylsalicyclic acid, should be avoided in patients with a history of myocardial infarctions, especially when they undergo surgical procedures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ASA, at a dose that inhibits NF-κB and blocks late PC, is not cardioprotective, whereas at a dose that does not inhibit NF-κB, ASA does not block late PC and is cardioprotective.
ASA in the dose of 5 mg/kg or 25 mg/kg has no effect on the activation of the transcription factor NF-kB and on the late PC effect against infarction.
the late PC effect is mediated through the activation of NF-kB and this activation can be blocked by ASA in a dose-dependent manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ASA may be a valuable tool for the study of late PC.
ASA may have a beneficial effect on late preconditioning against infarction in the myocardium.
ASA in a dose of 130 mg/kg completely abrogates late preconditioning against ischemia and reperfusion injury.
